Revisiting the Rally Car: The "Eyeball" Calculus

We have been having so much fun with all these functions and curves, reviewing our calculus, that we kind of forgot to follow up on the rally car data set I introduced on the first day. You have the data in front of you, and one thing we decided we were interested in getting was the average speed.

We already took the easy way in the homework, and honestly, given the chance, most of the time you should take the easy way. Why not? (Although sometimes you should do harder things for longer-term benefits, but I’m not here to lecture you on life choices today).

What almost all of you suggested was that we can just draw a horizontal line somewhere that seems to cut through the middle of the noisy speed data. We can eyeball the average speed. Once we have that average speed, we can figure out how long the driver has driven, which gives us the total displacement during the race.

During the race, the speed fluctuates a lot. But if we eyeball the average speed, we might call it 110 or 120 kilometers per hour. Let’s be generous and use 120. We denote average speed using pointy brackets, \langle v \rangle, or sometimes with a bar over the variable, \bar{v}.

\begin{equation} \langle v \rangle = 120 \text{ km/h} \tag{1} \end{equation}

To figure out how long this race was, we just multiply this average speed by the total time duration of the race, which we will call t_{\text{tot}}. The total displacement, x_{\text{tot}}, is:

\begin{equation} x_{\text{tot}} = \langle v \rangle \times t_{\text{tot}} \tag{2} \end{equation}

The idea here is that we are just calculating the area enclosed by a giant rectangle. We are taking a complicated, jagged shape with a bunch of dips and peaks, and turning it into an equivalent rectangle that has more or less the same area. Our human vision and intuition are pretty amazing at doing this visually.

Let’s do the math. The driver was driving for about 210 seconds.

\begin{equation} x_{\text{tot}} \approx 120 \text{ km/h} \times 210 \text{ s} \tag{3} \end{equation}

Unfortunately, the units of time do not match up. We need to take care of that. We know there are 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour, which means there are 3600 seconds in an hour. We can use this conversion factor so the units cancel out nicely.

\begin{align} x_{\text{tot}} &\approx 120 \frac{\text{km}}{\text{hr}} \times 210 \text{ s} \times \left( \frac{1 \text{ hr}}{3600 \text{ s}} \right) \label{eq:disp_converted} \\ x_{\text{tot}} &\approx \frac{120 \times 210}{3600} \text{ km} \tag{4} \end{align}

If you don’t have a calculator handy, this arithmetic might look annoying. Let’s just start rounding numbers to get a quick estimate. I will round 120 down to 100, 210 down to 200, and 3600 up to 4000.

\begin{equation} x_{\text{tot}} \approx \frac{100 \times 200}{4000} = \frac{20000}{4000} = 5 \text{ km} \tag{5} \end{equation}

Because I rounded the numerators down and the denominator up, this 5 km result is definitely an underestimate. The actual answer is closer to 7 km, which makes sense—we probably underestimated by 20 to 30 percent.

The Rigorous Way: Numerical Integration

The eyeballing method is great for a quick check, but there is a harder, more rigorous way to do this. From physics and calculus, we know that displacement x(t) is the integral of velocity v(t) with respect to time t:

\begin{equation} x(t) = \int v(t) dt \tag{6} \end{equation}

An integral is nothing but the area under the curve. If you are not keen on eyeballing a single giant rectangle, you can do it rigorously by chopping the funky shape up into a bunch of skinny rectangles.

Actually, a rectangle assumes the speed is constant over that tiny time step. A more accurate shape to draw is a trapezoid. A trapezoid is like a rectangle, but the top has a little bit of a slope to connect the data points. This is what they mean in calculus when they introduce the "Trapezoidal Rule."

The idea is that you feed your function through a shredder. You chop it up into arbitrarily skinny trapezoids, calculate the area of each one, and then add up all those tiny areas to get the total integral. We are going to have a computer do that tedious addition for us today.

Finding Acceleration: Group Strategy

We have quantified the average speed and the total displacement. What else are we interested in finding out quantitatively from this speed versus time data? Acceleration.

Specifically, I want to know: what is the maximum acceleration the driver experiences, expressed in multiples of g (gravitational acceleration)? We talked about g-forces previously when discussing fighter pilots.

If you were allowed to use any tool available, including a computer, how would you go about doing this? Let’s break down the plan.

First, we need to find the greatest change in speed over a time interval. If two adjacent speed numbers are close, the acceleration is low. If there is a huge jump in speed between two data points, that indicates a large acceleration. We are essentially looking for the maximum slope.

Second, we have a unit problem. We all know that g is approximately 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2.

\begin{equation} g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2 \tag{7} \end{equation}

Our data is in kilometers per hour. It would be highly helpful to convert the speed into a consistent unit system, specifically meters per second, before doing anything else.

So, our step-by-step plan is:

  1. Convert units: Change speed from km/h to m/s.

  2. Calculate slope: Find the change in speed over the change in time (\Delta v / \Delta t) for every point to get acceleration as a function of time, a(t).

  3. Find the maximum: Locate the highest value in that acceleration data.

  4. Convert to Gs: Divide that maximum acceleration by 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2.

Of course, Step 0 is feeding the data into a computer. We could calculate the rise over run by hand for every single sample point, but none of us want to do that. This is where our buddy Python comes into play.

Computer Calculus with Python

I asked you all to download the CSV data file and a Python script, and upload them into a new Google Colab notebook.

If you run into an error right away, it is likely because the file name in the script doesn’t match the file name of the data you uploaded. I was too lazy to change the script from last semester, so you just need to update the date in the file name string on line 7.

You will notice lines in the code that start with a hashtag (‘#‘). Python ignores whatever comes after the hashtag on that line. These are called comments. They are documentation for us humans, describing what the code is doing in plain English.

Here is the script we are running. I want you to pay special attention to how it executes our plan: it divides by 3.6 to convert km/h to m/s, uses ‘np.gradient‘ to find the slope (acceleration), and uses ‘cumulative_trapezoid‘ to add up the area under the curve (displacement).

Show Python code
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import cumulative_trapezoid

# 1. Load the data from the CSV file
df = pd.read_csv('260831 rally car data.csv')

# 2. Convert speed from km/h to m/s
df['Speed (m/s)'] = df['Speed (km/h)'] / 3.6

# 3. Calculate acceleration (m/s^2) using numerical gradient
# np.gradient uses second-order accurate central differences
df['Acceleration (m/s^2)'] = np.gradient(df['Speed (m/s)'], df['Time (s)'])

# 4. Calculate displacement (m) using numerical integration (trapezoidal rule)
# We assume the car starts at displacement = 0
df['Displacement (m)'] = cumulative_trapezoid(df['Speed (m/s)'], df['Time (s)'], initial=0)

# Helper variables for plotting
time = df['Time (s)']
speed_ms = df['Speed (m/s)']
accel = df['Acceleration (m/s^2)']
displacement = df['Displacement (m)']
mask_10s = (time % 10 == 0)

# --- Plot 1: Speed (km/h) vs Time ---
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(time, df['Speed (km/h)'], label='Speed (km/h)', color='blue')
plt.xlabel('Time (s)')
plt.ylabel('Speed (km/h)')
plt.title('Rally Car Speed (km/h) vs Time')
plt.grid(True)
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('speed_kmh.png')

# --- Plot 2: Speed (m/s) vs Time ---
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(time, speed_ms, label='Speed (m/s)', color='red')
plt.xlabel('Time (s)')
plt.ylabel('Speed (m/s)')
plt.title('Rally Car Speed (m/s) vs Time')
plt.grid(True)
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('speed_ms.png')

# --- Plot 3: Acceleration (m/s^2) vs Time ---
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
# All points: empty circles connected by lines
plt.plot(time, accel, color='green', marker='o', markerfacecolor='none', 
         markeredgecolor='green', markersize=4, linestyle='-', label='Acceleration')
# 10s intervals: black filled circles
plt.plot(time[mask_10s], accel[mask_10s], color='black', marker='o', 
         markerfacecolor='black', linestyle='None', label='Intervals (10s)')
plt.xlabel('Time (s)')
plt.ylabel('Acceleration (m/s$^{2}$)')
plt.title('Rally Car Acceleration vs Time')
plt.grid(True)
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('acceleration_vs_time.png')

# --- Plot 4: Speed (m/s) with Tangent Line Segments ---
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(time, speed_ms, color='red', label='Speed (m/s)', alpha=0.6)
dt_seg = 2.5 # Length of tangent segment for visualization
for t0 in time[mask_10s]:
    idx = df[df['Time (s)'] == t0].index[0]
    v0 = speed_ms[idx]
    a0 = accel[idx]
    
    # Define tangent line: v = a0*(t - t0) + v0
    t_seg = np.array([t0 - dt_seg, t0 + dt_seg])
    v_seg = a0 * (t_seg - t0) + v0
    
    plt.plot(t_seg, v_seg, color='black', linewidth=1.5)
    plt.plot(t0, v0, marker='o', color='black', markerfacecolor='black')
plt.xlabel('Time (s)')
plt.ylabel('Speed (m/s)')
plt.title('Speed (m/s) with Tangent Line Segments (every 10s)')
plt.grid(True)
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('speed_ms_with_tangents.png')

# --- Plot 5: Displacement (m) vs Time ---
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(time, displacement, color='purple', label='Displacement (m)')
plt.xlabel('Time (s)')
plt.ylabel('Displacement (m)')
plt.title('Rally Car Displacement (Distance Travelled) vs Time')
plt.grid(True)
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('displacement_vs_time.png')

print(f"Total distance travelled: {displacement.iloc[-1]:.2f} meters.")

Once you run this, it spits out a bunch of PNG image files. The first two plots simply show our raw data, first in km/h, and then scaled down into m/s.

The next set of plots is where the calculus happens. I wanted a visual indicator that the program was actually calculating the slope correctly. So, I had the script draw tangent line segments every 10 seconds on top of the speed curve.

You can visually see where the acceleration tends to be largest by looking for the steepest tangent lines. The bottom plot graphs that slope directly. Looking at the acceleration plot, we can see peaks approaching 10 \text{ m/s}^2, which means the driver is pulling around 1g of acceleration and deceleration.

Dynamic Visualization and the Role of AI

We can take this a step further and animate the data to watch the displacement accumulate over time. Here is a second script that generates a dynamic video of the race progress.

Show Python code
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import cv2
import os
from scipy.integrate import cumulative_trapezoid

# 1. Load the data
df = pd.read_csv('260323 rally car data.csv')

# 2. Convert km/h to km/s
df['Speed (km/s)'] = df['Speed (km/h)'] / 3600.0

# 3. Calculate displacement (numerical integral)
df['Displacement (km)'] = cumulative_trapezoid(df['Speed (km/s)'], df['Time (s)'], initial=0)

# 4. Define constant for Speed Y-axis (for consistent visual scale)
max_speed_global = df['Speed (km/s)'].max() * 1.1

if not os.path.exists('dynamic_frames'):
    os.makedirs('dynamic_frames')

frame_files = []

# 5. Generate frames with dynamic ranges
for t_idx in range(1, len(df)):
    t_val = df.iloc[t_idx]['Time (s)']
    current_df = df.iloc[:t_idx+1]
    
    # Dynamic Limits
    # X-axis: starts at 10, grows with current time
    x_limit = max(10, t_val)
    # Displacement Y-axis: starts at 0.1, grows with max displacement seen so far
    current_max_disp = current_df['Displacement (km)'].max()
    y_limit_disp = max(0.1, current_max_disp * 1.1)
    
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(8, 8))
    
    # Top Graph: Speed vs Time
    ax1.plot(current_df['Time (s)'], current_df['Speed (km/s)'], color='blue')
    ax1.fill_between(current_df['Time (s)'], current_df['Speed (km/s)'], color='blue', alpha=0.3)
    ax1.set_ylabel('Speed (km/s)')
    ax1.set_xlim(0, x_limit)
    ax1.set_ylim(0, max_speed_global)
    ax1.set_title(f'Rally Car Progress - Time: {t_val}s')
    ax1.grid(True)
    
    # Bottom Graph: Displacement vs Time
    ax2.plot(current_df['Time (s)'], current_df['Displacement (km)'], color='red')
    ax2.set_xlabel('Time (s)')
    ax2.set_ylabel('Displacement (km)')
    ax2.set_xlim(0, x_limit)
    ax2.set_ylim(0, y_limit_disp)
    ax2.grid(True)
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    filename = f'dynamic_frames/frame_{t_idx:03d}.png'
    plt.savefig(filename)
    frame_files.append(filename)
    plt.close()

# 6. Compile images into a single video
output_video = 'rally_car_dynamic_animation.mp4'
frame = cv2.imread(frame_files[0])
height, width, layers = frame.shape
fourcc = cv2.VideoWriter_fourcc(*'mp4v')
video = cv2.VideoWriter(output_video, fourcc, 10, (width, height))

for image_file in frame_files:
    video.write(cv2.imread(image_file))

video.release()
